hmmt-feb-2006-team1-01.title: Count by the east and west mobots
hmmt-feb-2006-team1-01.body:
A mobot oriented north or south mows only its own clump. A west-oriented mobot starting on clump $a$ mows clumps $1,\dots,a$, and an east-oriented mobot starting on clump $n-b+1$ mows the last $b$ clumps. There can be at most one west-oriented and at most one east-oriented mobot (two of them would overlap). Let the west mobot mow $a\ge0$ clumps and the east mobot $b\ge0$ clumps ($a=0$ or $b=0$ meaning there is none). Then $a+b\le n$, and each of the other $n-a-b$ clumps has a single north- or south-oriented mobot: $2^{n-a-b}$ ways. Hence the number of formations is
$$\sum_{a=0}^{n}\sum_{b=0}^{n-a}2^{n-a-b}=\sum_{a=0}^{n}\left(2^{n-a+1}-1\right)=\left(2^{n+2}-2\right)-(n+1)=2^{n+2}-n-3.$$

(Check: $n=1$ gives $4$ formations, one for each direction.)

**Answer: $2^{n+2}-n-3$**

hmmt-feb-2006-team1-02.title: Peel off the corner
hmmt-feb-2006-team1-02.body:
Let $F(m,n)$ be the number of allowable formations on an $m\times n$ lawn, with $F(m,0)=F(0,n)=1$ (empty lawn, empty formation). Suppose $m,n\ge1$. The clump $(0,0)$ can only be mowed by a mobot that starts on it (no mobot moves south or west), oriented north or east.

- If it is oriented **north**, it mows the whole column $x=0$. No other mobot can start in column $0$ (it would mow a clump of that column twice), and no mobot outside that column ever enters it (mobots move only north or east, staying in their column or moving away). So the rest of the formation is an allowable formation of the remaining $m\times(n-1)$ lawn (columns $1,\dots,n-1$), and conversely any such formation together with this mobot works: $F(m,n-1)$ ways.
- If it is oriented **east**, it mows the whole row $y=0$, and in the same way the rest is an allowable formation of the $(m-1)\times n$ lawn (rows $1,\dots,m-1$): $F(m-1,n)$ ways.

Thus $F(m,n)=F(m,n-1)+F(m-1,n)$ with the boundary values $1$. The numbers $\binom{m+n}{m}$ satisfy the same recursion (Pascal's rule) and the same boundary values, so by induction on $m+n$, $F(m,n)=\binom{m+n}{m}=\frac{(m+n)!}{m!\,n!}$. ∎

(Equivalently: the starting points of the mobots form a lattice path, which corresponds to choosing which $m$ of $m+n$ steps go up.)

hmmt-feb-2006-team1-03.title: Same recursion, new boundary
hmmt-feb-2006-team1-03.body:
Let $N(m,n)$ be the number of formations on the trapezoid with columns $x=0,\dots,n-1$ of heights $m+1-n+x$ (valid for $m\ge n-1$; when $m=n-1$ the column $x=0$ has height $0$). Put $f(m,n)=\binom{m+n}{m}-\binom{m+n}{m+2}$.

**Recursion.** Suppose $m\ge n\ge1$, so column $0$ is nonempty. Exactly as in the rectangle, the clump $(0,0)$ is mowed by a mobot starting there, oriented north or east.
- North: it mows column $0$, and the rest is a formation on columns $1,\dots,n-1$, whose heights $m+1-n+x$ ($x\ge1$) are those of $N(m,n-1)$ (shift $x\to x-1$: heights $m+1-(n-1)+x'$). So $N(m,n-1)$ ways.
- East: it mows the bottom row $y=0$ (all $n$ columns have height $\ge1$), and the rest, after shifting down by $1$, has column heights $m-n+x=(m-1)+1-n+x$, which is the lawn of $N(m-1,n)$ (valid as $m-1\ge n-1$). So $N(m-1,n)$ ways.
Hence $N(m,n)=N(m,n-1)+N(m-1,n)$ for $m\ge n\ge1$, and $N(m,0)=1$.

**The formula.** $f$ satisfies Pascal's rule: $\binom{m+n}{m}=\binom{m+n-1}{m}+\binom{m+n-1}{m-1}$ and $\binom{m+n}{m+2}=\binom{m+n-1}{m+2}+\binom{m+n-1}{m+1}$, so $f(m,n)=f(m,n-1)+f(m-1,n)$; also $f(m,0)=1-0=1$. The recursion only uses values with $m\ge n-1$, except that at $m=n-1$ the column $0$ is empty and the lawn is the same as for $N(n-1,n-1)$ (drop the empty column), so we need $f(n-1,n)=f(n-1,n-1)$: indeed $f(n-1,n)-f(n-1,n-1)=\binom{2n-2}{n-2}-\binom{2n-2}{n}=0$ by symmetry of binomial coefficients (using Pascal on both terms). By induction on $m+n$, $N(m,n)=f(m,n)=\binom{m+n}{m}-\binom{m+n}{m+2}$. ∎

(Equivalently, formations correspond to up/right lattice paths from $(0,0)$ to $(n,m)$ that stay below a line, counted by the reflection principle: the bad paths number $\binom{m+n}{m+2}$.)

**Answer: $\binom{m+n}{m}-\binom{m+n}{m+2}$**

hmmt-feb-2006-team1-04.title: Upper bound and a reduction
hmmt-feb-2006-team1-04.body:
$n$ mobots suffice: put one at the left end of each row, oriented east.

For the lower bound, call the three directions east, NW ($30^\circ$ west of north, moving up-left) and SW ($30^\circ$ west of south, moving down-left). Number the rows $1$ (top) to $n$ (bottom). These directions are along the three families of lattice lines, and each mobot stops at the boundary: an east mobot at the right edge, a NW mobot at the left edge, a SW mobot at the bottom row. Let $m(n)$ be the minimum number of mobots for the triangle $T_n$; $m(1)=1$.

**Lemma.** If a formation $F$ of $T_n$ ($n\ge2$) contains a mobot that starts in the bottom row and is oriented east or SW, then there is a formation of $T_{n-1}$ (the top $n-1$ rows) with at most $|F|-1$ mobots.
*Proof.* Such a mobot mows only bottom-row clumps. Remove all mobots that start in the bottom row and are oriented east or SW. Replace each NW mobot starting in the bottom row by the mobot starting one step further (in row $n-1$), or delete it if that point is off the lawn (this happens for the bottom-left corner). Keep every other mobot; a SW mobot starting above simply stops when it leaves $T_{n-1}$. Every clump of $T_{n-1}$ is still mowed exactly once, and at least the given mobot was removed. ∎

**Induction.** Let $Q$ be the bottom-right corner clump. The only mobots that can mow it are: an east mobot starting in the bottom row, a SW mobot starting at $Q$, or a NW mobot starting at $Q$ (which then mows the entire right edge). In the first two cases the Lemma gives $|F|\ge m(n-1)+1$. In the third case, rotate the picture by $120^\circ$ so that the right edge becomes the bottom row; the rotation permutes the three allowed directions cyclically, so the rotated formation is again a formation of $T_n$, now with an east mobot mowing the entire bottom row, and the Lemma applies again. So $m(n)\ge m(n-1)+1$, hence $m(n)\ge n$. Together with the construction, $m(n)=n$.

**Answer: $n$**

hmmt-feb-2006-team1-05.title: Central clumps
hmmt-feb-2006-team1-05.body:
Put the lawn in barycentric form: the points are $(i,j,k)$ with $i,j,k\ge0$, $i+j+k=n-1$, and the $120^\circ$ rotation is the cyclic shift $(i,j,k)\mapsto(k,i,j)$, which permutes the three mobot directions cyclically.

**$n\equiv1\pmod3$:** the center $\left(\frac{n-1}3,\frac{n-1}3,\frac{n-1}3\right)$ is a clump. The mobot mowing it either starts there (then its orientation would have to be invariant under a $120^\circ$ rotation - impossible), or starts elsewhere; but then its three rotated copies are three different mobots that all mow the center. So there are no happy formations: answer $0$.

**$n\not\equiv1\pmod3$:** there are three clumps equally close to the center, permuted by the rotation. Considering how they can be mowed, one sees that a mobot starts at each of the three, and (in two possible ways, according to their orientations) they cut the rest of the lawn into three congruent pieces permuted by the rotation. Each piece is a trapezoid as in problem 3 (with the same allowed directions). A happy formation is determined by a formation of one piece (the other two are its rotated copies), and any formation of one piece extends. So the answer is the sum, over the two ways of orienting the central mobots, of the number of formations of one trapezoid.

- $n\equiv0\pmod3$: the pieces are $\left(\frac{2n}3,\frac{n-3}3\right)$-trapezoids or $\left(\frac{2n-3}3,\frac n3\right)$-trapezoids, giving $\binom{n-1}{2n/3}-\binom{n-1}{(2n+6)/3}+\binom{n-1}{(2n-3)/3}-\binom{n-1}{(2n+3)/3}$.
- $n\equiv2\pmod3$: the pieces are $\left(\frac{2n-1}3,\frac{n-2}3\right)$- or $\left(\frac{2n-4}3,\frac{n+1}3\right)$-trapezoids, giving $\binom{n-1}{(2n-1)/3}-\binom{n-1}{(2n+5)/3}+\binom{n-1}{(2n-4)/3}-\binom{n-1}{(2n+2)/3}$.

(Check against direct enumeration: $n=2,3,5,6$ give $2,3,9,14$; $n=1,4,7$ give $0$.)

hmmt-feb-2006-team1-06.title: Parallel classes
hmmt-feb-2006-team1-06.body:
Label the vertices $0,1,\dots,n-1$ around the circle. The chord joining $i$ and $j$ is perpendicular to the direction at angle $\frac{\pi(i+j)}{n}$ (from the center), so two chords are parallel iff $i+j\equiv i'+j'\pmod n$. Hence the chords (sides and diagonals) fall into exactly $n$ parallel classes, indexed by $s=i+j\bmod n$, and no two diagonals from different classes are parallel. So at most $n$ diagonals can be drawn with no two parallel.

It remains to show that every class contains a diagonal (then we pick one from each class). The pairs in class $s$ are $\{i,s-i\}$ with difference $s-2i$; it is a diagonal iff $s-2i\not\equiv0,\pm1\pmod n$. For $n$ odd, $s-2i$ takes all residues, and $n\ge5$ leaves some residue outside $\{0,\pm1\}$. For $n$ even, $s-2i$ ranges over the $\frac n2\ge3$ residues of the same parity as $s$; if $s$ is even we need a nonzero even residue, and if $s$ is odd an odd residue other than $\pm1$, and either exists since $\frac n2\ge3$. So $n$ diagonals can be drawn. ∎

**Answer: $n$**

hmmt-feb-2006-team1-07.title: Reduction and upper bound
hmmt-feb-2006-team1-07.body:
Whether two diagonals meet (cross in the interior or share an endpoint) depends only on the cyclic order of the endpoints, so we may assume the polygon is regular. For $n=4$ there are only $2$ diagonals, and they cross: answer $2$.

Let $n\ge5$. Two parallel diagonals of a regular polygon neither cross nor share a vertex, so a valid set has no two parallel diagonals, and by the previous problem it has at most $n$ diagonals.

**Construction.** Say two vertices are $k$ apart if there are $k$ steps between them the short way. Two disjoint, non-crossing chords with endpoints in cyclic order $a,b,c,d$ (chords $ab$ and $cd$) have arcs $x=b-a$, $y=d-c$ not containing the other chord, and $x+y\le n-2$ (at least one step between $b$ and $c$, and between $d$ and $a$). So if both chords have both arcs $\ge\frac n2-1$, then $x=y=\frac n2-1$ with gaps exactly $1$, which makes the chords parallel.
- $n$ odd: draw the $n$ diagonals joining vertices that are $\frac{n-1}2$ apart. Both arcs of each are $\ge\frac{n-1}2>\frac n2-1$, so any two of them cross or share a vertex.
- $n$ even ($n\ge6$): draw the $\frac n2$ diameters, and the $n$ diagonals joining vertices $\frac n2-1$ apart come in $\frac n2$ pairs of parallel chords; take one from each pair. Any two of the chosen chords either cross, share a vertex, or would be parallel by the remark above, and we took no parallel pair.

So $n$ diagonals can be drawn, and the maximum is $n$ for $n\ge5$ and $2$ for $n=4$. ∎

**Answer: $2$ if $n=4$, otherwise $n$**

hmmt-feb-2006-team1-08.title: Circumradius
hmmt-feb-2006-team1-08.body:
Let $R=\frac1{2\sin(\pi/n)}$ be the circumradius (the side length is $2R\sin\frac\pi n=1$). With $r=R$ all circles pass through the center, so the intersection is non-empty.

Conversely, suppose a point $P$ lies within distance $r$ of every vertex $V_i$ (even in all the closed *disks*). Let $O$ be the center; $\sum_i\vec{OV_i}=\vec0$ by symmetry, so
$$\sum_{i=1}^n|PV_i|^2=\sum_i\left(|PO|^2+|OV_i|^2\right)=n|PO|^2+nR^2\ge nR^2.$$
Thus the average of $|PV_i|^2$ is at least $R^2$, so some $|PV_i|\ge R$, whence $r\ge R$. (For the cross terms: $\sum_i 2\,\vec{PO}\cdot\vec{OV_i}=0$.) Hence the smallest radius is $R$.

**Answer: $r=\frac12\csc\frac{180^\circ}n$**

hmmt-feb-2006-team1-09.title: Induction on $n$
hmmt-feb-2006-team1-09.body:
For $n=3$, the angles sum to $180^\circ$ and a triangle with those angles exists.

Let $n\ge4$ and assume the statement for $n-1$. If $n=4$ and $\theta_1=\theta_3=180^\circ-\theta_2=180^\circ-\theta_4$, a parallelogram works, so assume this is not the case.

*Claim:* two adjacent angles (cyclically) have sum $>180^\circ$. If not, $\theta_i+\theta_{i+1}\le180^\circ$ for all $i$ (indices mod $n$); summing, $2\cdot180(n-2)\le180n$, i.e. $n\le4$. So $n=4$ and equality holds everywhere, which forces $\theta_1=\theta_3$, $\theta_2=\theta_4$, $\theta_1+\theta_2=180^\circ$: the excluded parallelogram case.

Relabel so that $\theta_{n-1}+\theta_n>180^\circ$ and put $\theta'=\theta_{n-1}+\theta_n-180^\circ$; then $0<\theta'<180^\circ$ and $\theta_1,\dots,\theta_{n-2},\theta'$ are $n-1$ angles in $(0,180^\circ)$ with sum $180(n-2)-180=180(n-3)$. By the induction hypothesis there is a convex $(n-1)$-gon with these angles in order. At the vertex $V$ with angle $\theta'$, cut off a small triangle $VXY$ ($X,Y$ on the two sides at $V$, close to $V$, with the angle at $X$ equal to $180^\circ-\theta_{n-1}$ and at $Y$ equal to $180^\circ-\theta_n$, which is possible since $\theta'+(180^\circ-\theta_{n-1})+(180^\circ-\theta_n)=180^\circ$). Replacing $V$ by $X,Y$ gives an $n$-gon whose interior angles at $X$ and $Y$ are $\theta_{n-1}$ and $\theta_n$ and whose other angles are unchanged. It is convex since all angles are less than $180^\circ$. ∎

hmmt-feb-2006-team1-10.title: Exterior angles
hmmt-feb-2006-team1-10.body:
Work with exterior angles $180^\circ-\theta_i$. They are distinct positive integers (at most $179$) and sum to $360$. Since $1+2+\cdots+27=378>360$, at most $26$ distinct positive integers can sum to $360$: $n\le26$.

For $n=26$ take the exterior angles $1,2,\dots,25$ (sum $325$) and $35$: the sum is $360$, all are distinct and between $1$ and $179$. The interior angles $179,178,\dots,155,145$ are distinct integers less than $180$ with sum $180\cdot26-360=180(26-2)$, so by the previous problem a convex $26$-gon with exactly these angles exists. ∎

**Answer: 26**

hmmt-feb-2006-team1-11.title: Forced coloring
hmmt-feb-2006-team1-11.body:
It can be red: color each card by its first digit ($1$ red, $2$ yellow, $3$ blue); this satisfies all the conditions.

Now we show it must be red. A card differing from $122\,222\,222$ (red) and from $222\,222\,222$ (yellow) in every digit cannot be red or yellow, so it is blue. The cards $333\,133\,133$ and $331\,331\,331$ differ from both in all digits, so both are **blue**. The card $211\,311\,311$ differs in all digits from $122\,222\,222$ (red) and from $333\,133\,133$ (blue), so it is **yellow**. Finally $123\,123\,123$ differs in all digits from $331\,331\,331$ (blue) and from $211\,311\,311$ (yellow), so it can only be **red**. ∎

**Answer: red**

hmmt-feb-2006-team1-12.title: Rows of cubes
hmmt-feb-2006-team1-12.body:
Orient the cube along the axes. An *$x$-row* is a set of three unit cubes whose centers differ only in the $x$-coordinate; there are $9$ $x$-rows, and similarly $9$ $y$-rows and $9$ $z$-rows.

**Achieving 50.** Remove one $x$-row and one $y$-row meeting in a corner cube, e.g. $\{(0,0,0),(1,0,0),(2,0,0),(0,1,0),(0,2,0)\}$: $3+3-1=5$ cubes. Now $8$ of the $x$-rows, $8$ of the $y$-rows and all $9$ $z$-rows are non-empty, and each non-empty row is a contiguous block of cubes, so it contributes exactly $2$ faces perpendicular to its direction: surface area $2(8+8+9)=50$.

**Lower bound.** Each $x$-row that still contains at least one cube contributes at least $2$ unit faces perpendicular to the $x$-direction (an entry and an exit face along that line); similarly for $y$- and $z$-rows. So the surface area is at least $2\times$(number of non-empty rows). Two completely removed rows in the same direction would remove $6$ cubes, so at most one row per direction is completely removed; and removing one row of each of the three directions would remove at least $7$ cubes. Hence at most $2$ rows are completely removed, at least $27-2=25$ rows are non-empty, and the surface area is at least $2\cdot25=50$. ∎

**Answer: 50**

hmmt-feb-2006-team1-13.title: Compute the signed area
hmmt-feb-2006-team1-13.body:
Take the squares to be unit squares, colored by $c(x,y)=s(x)s(y)$ with $s(x)=(-1)^{\lfloor x\rfloor}$, so the (red minus black) area covered by the disk $D$ of radius $\rho<\frac12$ and center $(a,b)$ is $g=\iint_Dc$. We show: if $a$ and $b$ are not integers, then $g\ne0$.

Since the diameter is below $1$, the disk meets at most one vertical grid line $x=p$ and at most one horizontal grid line $y=q$.
- *Neither line:* $D$ lies inside one square, so $g=\pm\text{area}(D)\ne0$.
- *Only a vertical line $x=p$:* $c(x,y)=\pm\operatorname{sign}(x-p)$ on $D$, so $|g|=|A_{\text{right}}-A_{\text{left}}|$, the difference of the areas on the two sides of the line. The side containing the center has the larger area (the center is not on the line), so $g\ne0$. Same for a horizontal line only.
- *Both lines:* by reflecting the board we may assume $a>p$ and $b>q$, and $|g|=\left|\iint_D u(x)v(y)\right|$ with $u=\operatorname{sign}(x-p)$, $v=\operatorname{sign}(y-q)$. Reflect $D$ in the line $x=p$ to get $D'$ with center $(2p-a,b)$. For $x>p$ the point $(x,y)$ is closer to $(a,b)$ than to $(2p-a,b)$, so $D'\cap\{x>p\}\subseteq D\cap\{x>p\}$, and the part of $D$ left of $p$ cancels with its mirror image inside the right part (since $v$ does not depend on $x$). Hence $\iint_Du\,v=\iint_Rv$, where $R=(D\cap\{x>p\})\setminus D'$ is a lune that is symmetric about the line $y=b$ and has positive area, including points arbitrarily close to $y=b$. Because $R$ is symmetric about $y=b$ and $b>q$, $\iint_Rv=A(R)-2A(R\cap\{y<b\}\cap\{y<q\})$, and $A(R\cap\{y<b,y<q\})<A(R\cap\{y<b\})=\frac12A(R)$ since $R\cap\{q<y<b\}$ has positive area. So $\iint_Rv>0$ and $g\ne0$.

Hence a checker with $g=0$ must have an integer center coordinate: its center lies on a boundary between squares or at a junction of four. ∎

hmmt-feb-2006-team1-14.title: Reduce to a finite check
hmmt-feb-2006-team1-14.body:
If $(a,b)$ is a solution then so is $(b,a)$, so a unique solution has $a=b$, and then $n=2a$ is even. If $n=2a\ge12$, then $x=a-1\ge5$, $y=a+1\ge7$ gives another solution: $\left\lfloor\frac{(a-1)^2}{a+1}\right\rfloor+\left\lfloor\frac{(a+1)^2}{a-1}\right\rfloor=\left\lfloor a-3+\frac4{a+1}\right\rfloor+\left\lfloor a+3+\frac4{a-1}\right\rfloor=(a-3)+(a+3)=2a$. So $n$ is not bummed out. Also $n=4$ has the solutions $(2,2)$ and $(1,2)$. Remaining candidates: $2,6,8,10$.

For these, a solution satisfies $n=\lfloor x^2/y\rfloor+\lfloor y^2/x\rfloor>\frac{x^2}{2y}+\frac{x^2}{2y}+\frac{y^2}{x}-2\ge\frac{3x}{\sqrt[3]4}-2$ (AM-GM), so $x<\frac{\sqrt[3]4}{3}(n+2)<0.53(n+2)\le6.4$, so $x\le6$, and likewise $y\le6$. The values of $\lfloor x^2/y\rfloor+\lfloor y^2/x\rfloor$ for $1\le x,y\le6$ (row $x$, column $y$):
$$\begin{array}{c|cccccc}&1&2&3&4&5&6\\\hline1&2&4&9&16&25&36\\2&4&4&5&9&12&18\\3&9&5&6&7&9&13\\4&16&9&7&8&9&11\\5&25&12&9&9&10&11\\6&36&18&13&11&11&12\end{array}$$
The value $2$ occurs only for $(1,1)$, $6$ only for $(3,3)$, $8$ only for $(4,4)$, and $10$ only for $(5,5)$. So these four are bummed out. ∎

**Answer: 2, 6, 8, 10**

hmmt-feb-2006-team1-15.title: Criterion
hmmt-feb-2006-team1-15.body:
Let $N=\sum_{i=0}^da_i10^i$ be a palindrome ($a_i=a_{d-i}$, $a_d\ne0$) and $b_k=\sum_{i+j=k}a_ia_j$ for $0\le k\le2d$, so $N^2=\sum b_k10^k$ (not yet the decimal expansion), $b_k=b_{2d-k}$ and $b_d=\sum a_i^2$. **Claim: $N^2$ is a palindrome iff $\sum_i a_i^2<10$.**

**($\Leftarrow$)** By AM-GM, $b_k\le\sum_{i+j=k}\frac{a_i^2+a_j^2}2\le\sum_ia_i^2<10$, so no carries occur: the digits of $N^2$ are $b_0,\dots,b_{2d}$, which read the same backwards since $b_k=b_{2d-k}$.

**($\Rightarrow$)** Suppose $\sum a_i^2\ge10$, i.e. $b_d\ge10$, and $N^2$ is a palindrome; write $a=a_0=a_d$ and $e_k$ for the decimal digits of $N^2$, $e_k\equiv b_k+c_k\pmod{10}$ with carries $c_0=0$, $c_{k+1}=\lfloor(b_k+c_k)/10\rfloor$. The last digit of $N^2$ is $a^2\bmod10$.
*Case $a\ge4$.* $N\in[a\cdot10^d,(a+1)10^d)$, so $N^2\in[a^2,(a+1)^2)\cdot10^{2d}$. For $a=4,5,6,7,8,9$ the first digit of $N^2$ is in $\{1,2\},\{2,3\},\{3,4\},\{4,5,6\},\{6,7,8\},\{8,9\}$ respectively, while the last digit is $6,5,6,9,4,1$: never equal.
*Case $a\le3$.* Then $N^2<16\cdot10^{2d}$. If $N^2$ has $2d+2$ digits then $a=3$, the first digit is $1$ and the last is $9$: not a palindrome. So $N^2$ has $2d+1$ digits. Let $\ell\le2d$ be the largest index with $e_\ell\ne b_\ell$ (it exists: $e_d\ne b_d$ since $b_d\ge10$). For $k>\ell$: $e_k=b_k$, and the carries $c_k$ are $0$ (a nonzero carry would be a multiple of $10$, hence $\ge10$, and produce a carry out of the top, giving more than $2d+1$ digits). So $b_\ell+c_\ell\le9$, $c_\ell\ge1$, hence $b_\ell\le8$. By palindromicity $e_k=e_{2d-k}=b_{2d-k}=b_k$ for all $k<2d-\ell$, which forces (by induction, $c_0=0$) all carries $c_k=0$ for $k\le2d-\ell$, so $e_{2d-\ell}=b_{2d-\ell}\bmod10=b_\ell$ (as $b_\ell\le8$). But palindromicity gives $e_{2d-\ell}=e_\ell\ne b_\ell$. Contradiction. ∎

**Classification.** A palindrome with $\sum a_i^2\le9$ has digits symmetric in pairs (plus a middle digit if the length is odd). A single-digit palindrome: $1,2,3$. Otherwise the outer digit appears twice, so $2a_d^2\le9$ gives $a_d\in\{1,2\}$. If $a_d=2$ the outer pair uses $8$, leaving at most $1$: only zeros, or a single $1$ in the exact middle: $2\,0\cdots0\,2$ and $2\,0\cdots0\,1\,0\cdots0\,2$. If $a_d=1$: no digit $3$ is possible and a pair of $2$'s costs $8$ (too much with the outer pair), so the digits are $0$s and $1$s with at most nine $1$s, or a single $2$ in the middle (cost $4$) with at most four $1$s (two pairs) elsewhere. Together with the number $3$, this is the answer.

**Answer:** $3$; palindromes of $0$s and $1$s with at most nine $1$s; palindromes with a single $2$ in the middle and otherwise $0$s and at most four $1$s; $2\,0\cdots0\,2$; and $2\,0\cdots0\,1\,0\cdots0\,2$.
